reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: A ganglion is the commonest soft-tissue swelling of the hand and wrist, presenting as a smooth, firm, rounded lump that may fluctuate in size
The most frequent sites are the dorsal wrist (arising from the scapholunate region), the volar wrist, and the flexor tendon sheath of the fingers
The cyst contains a viscous, gelatinous mucin and typically transilluminates, which helps distinguish it from a solid mass
It arises from a joint capsule or tendon sheath and communicates with the joint through a valve-like stalk, so it is not a true cyst with an epithelial lining
Many are painless and diagnosed on appearance alone; discomfort, if present, relates to size, position, or pressure on adjacent structures
A small occult dorsal ganglion can cause wrist pain before it becomes visible and may only be found on imaging
Reassurance and observation are appropriate for most, as a significant proportion resolve spontaneously
Aspiration can relieve symptoms but recurrence is common, and the old practice of striking the cyst is not recommended
Surgical excision including the stalk and capsular origin gives the lowest recurrence rate but still carries a risk of recurrence and of scar or stiffness
reference.pathophysiology: A ganglion forms from mucoid degeneration of the connective tissue of a joint capsule or tendon sheath. Mucin accumulates to form a cyst that connects to the underlying joint via a tortuous, valve-like duct, allowing one-way flow of fluid that fills the cyst. It lacks a true synovial or epithelial lining. Local irritation or minor trauma may contribute, and the fluctuation in size reflects communication with the joint.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
Lipoma or other benign soft-tissue tumour
Aneurysm at the volar wrist (near the radial artery)
additionalInvestigations: Usually diagnosed clinically, aided by transillumination
Ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion, identify an occult ganglion, and assess its relation to vessels and tendons
MRI for occult, deep, or atypical swellings and to exclude other soft-tissue lesions
Consider vascular imaging for a pulsatile volar wrist mass before any intervention
Histology after excision to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed, or irregular mass suggesting a soft-tissue tumour
A pulsatile volar wrist swelling raising the possibility of an aneurysm
Neurological symptoms from compression of an adjacent nerve
Signs of infection or unexpected features prompting further imaging or biopsy
reference.prognosis: Ganglia are benign, and a large proportion resolve without treatment; aspiration has a high recurrence rate, and surgical excision reduces but does not eliminate recurrence.
pitfalls: Assuming any wrist lump is a ganglion and missing a tumour or aneurysm
Aspirating a volar wrist mass without first excluding a vascular lesion
Underestimating recurrence after aspiration or incomplete excision
Overlooking an occult dorsal ganglion as a cause of unexplained wrist pain
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Reassure and observe asymptomatic cysts, since a large proportion resolve spontaneously
Offer needle aspiration for symptomatic lesions, counselling that recurrence is frequent
Relieve discomfort with simple analgesia, activity modification and splinting
Undertake surgical excision of the cyst together with its capsular stalk for painful, recurrent or functionally limiting lesions, giving the lowest recurrence
Confirm arterial patency with an Allen test and image the radial artery before any volar wrist intervention
Counsel patients that recurrence remains possible even after meticulous excision
